course_description: Introduction to the peoples and cultures of Early Medieval England (c450-c1100), with primary emphasis on texts written in Old English and Latin. Interdisciplinary approach including history, literature, religion, and material culture. Attention to literary genres ranging from elegy to riddles; the development of Christianity; encounters with Romans, Vikings, and Normans; and other political and social concerns. All readings in translation.
course_summary: Explores the history, literature, religion, art, and culture of Early Medieval England through a variety of texts. Discusses the Christianization of England, conflicts with Vikings, and the Norman Conquest, along with modern adaptations of these stories.
learning_outcomes:
- Recognize and discuss major forms, techniques, social conditions, values, and genres that have shaped the history of English literature, language, and culture.

- Discern and integrate divergent and contradictory perspectives, identify and question assumptions, and assess evidence and methods related to Early Medieval England.

- Write original, coherent, and compelling arguments about assigned texts and/or objects that push beyond summary to analysis and independent and critical thinking in clear prose that meets expectations for grammatical correctness.
what_you_will_learn:
- Understand the origins of Early Medieval England and its Christianization.
- Explore literary works from the period in both Old English and Latin.
- Analyze major historical events such as the Viking invasions and the Norman Conquest.
- Understand contemporary adaptations of medieval literature.

schedule_of_topics.topic_name: The Early Medieval English: Origin Stories, Nostalgia, and the Past
readings_or_tasks: Map of Heptarchy in the Time of Bede (Higham and Ryan)*
Map of England c. 878; Map of Britain in the 10th century (Foot)*
“England before the Norman Conquest” and “The Normans and Feudalism” from the Broadview Anthology of British Literature Vol. 1 (pp. xxxii-xlii)*
Oosthuizen, “The Phrase ‘Anglo-Saxon’” (Emergence of the English pp. 3-6)*

schedule_of_topics.topic_name: Origin Stories, Nostalgia, and the Past, cont.
readings_or_tasks: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People (EH): Preface, I.1, I.12, I.14-16, I.22-23, II.9, II.12-14, II.20 (pp. 41-47; 58-60; 61-64; 72-73; 117-120; 125-32; 140-42)
Map of Migrations, 400-600* (again); Map of England and Wales c. 700 (Wiley-Blackwell)*
OPTIONAL: see these poems in their original manuscript forms at OEPF: Wanderer; Ruin.
The Dream of the Rood (Liuzza Anthology)
Images and Text of The Ruthwell Cross*

schedule_of_topics.topic_name: Care for Souls and Care for Bodies
readings_or_tasks: The Grave, Old English Soul and Body*
Old English Metrical Charms (Liuzza Anthology, pp. 77-86)
Wilson, “Anglo-Saxon remedy kills hospital superbug MRSA”
Wulf and Eadwacer, The Wife’s Lament (Liuzza Anthology)
Mittman and Kim, Wonders of the East (ROEP)
Early Medieval World Maps: a T-O Map, Cotton MS Tiberius B V, Psalter Map
Higham and Ryan, The Anglo-Saxon World, pp. 323-38 and 366-69*
Asser, Life of King Alfred, Chapters 35-43, 73-77, and 87-89*
Alfred, Preface to Pastoral Care and Preface to Augustine’s Soliloquies*
Higham and Ryan, The Anglo-Saxon World, pp. 235-39 and pp. 258-62*
William of Malmesbury’s Gesta Regum Anglorum (excerpt)*
Map of Britain in the tenth century (Foot) (again)*
